extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in literary criticism, playwrights, and writers of rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for composing and evaluating tragedy (drama) and persuasive discourse, drawing on Aristotle's Poetics and Rhetoric. Includes dramatic criteria (plot, mimesis, catharsis, plot devices) and rhetorical criteria (argumentation, appeals, delivery, civic purposes), plus editorial/edition-quality features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unities of action, place, and time
rubrics_metrics.description: The (often misunderstood) theory of the unities of action, place, and time as criteria for dramatic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle introduces the unities as principles for drama; these remain debated. The page notes the theory is often misunderstood and situates it among other lasting ideas from the Poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is a form of imitation; drama is an imitation of human actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This foundational claim frames how dramatic works should represent human action and behavior — i.e., verisimilitude, representation of motive and consequence, and the ethical/psychological realism of characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the central element of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the drama's central element and should drive the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasizes plot over other elements (character, diction, etc.). He applies this principle in analyses of classic Greek dramas (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides), showing how coherent causal sequence and structure determine a play's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal and recognition as important plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis) are important elements within a plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices — a sudden change in fortune and a critical identification/insight — are highlighted as mechanisms that produce tragic effect when properly integrated into the plot's causal chain. Aristotle illustrates their role via examples from Greek tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (purging of pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of tragedy is the purging (catharsis) of pity and fear from the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should evoke and then purge these emotions, producing a moral/psychological effect; this purpose is central to evaluating tragic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentation and logical development of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical practice requires argumentation and the logical development of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats the construction of demonstrative and persuasive proofs as a core rhetorical skill — assessing claims, structuring reasons, and developing lines of proof appropriate to context and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to emotion (pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective rhetoric includes appeals to emotion as a means of persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to the audience's emotions are a distinct pillar of rhetoric; their ethical and tactical deployment is part of evaluating persuasive effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matters of delivery and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery and style are key components of rhetorical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How something is said (diction, arrangement, presentation, and delivery) affects persuasive power; style and performance/delivery should suit the purpose and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric's civic functions (accusing, defending, recommending policy, proving/refuting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric is the art of engaging in civic activities: accusing and defending, recommending policies, and proving and refuting ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames rhetoric as central to public life; evaluating rhetorical work therefore includes assessing how well it fulfills these civic purposes and adapts to genre-specific aims (forensic, deliberative, epideictic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Edition features / scholarly apparatus (introductions, notes, bibliographies, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial and design features that make an edition useful to students and general readers: new introductions, biographies, chronologies, footnotes and endnotes, selective discussions, comments by other authors, study questions, bibliographies, indices & glossaries, and illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Barnes & Noble Classics series emphasizes scholarship and reading aids: commissioned introductions, contextual materials, explanatory apparatus, and careful design/printing. These editorial elements are criteria for the quality and usefulness of a published edition for teaching and study.
